{"id": "20:3/q09", "question": "How do verses 2 and 3 console the Prophet about the Quran's burden?", "turns_on": "Whether the hardship denied is grief over disbelief, strain in worship, or the inevitable work of proclamation.", "positions": [{"id": "20:3/q09/p1", "position": "His duty is to convey the reminder; he need not exhaust himself over others' rejection.", "reasons": "Razi cites 18:6 and 10:65: each person's belief concerns that person. Maqatil says revelation was not meant to make Muhammad suffer."}, {"id": "20:3/q09/p2", "position": "The Quran is for reminder, so the Prophet should not harm himself through excessive worship or hardship.", "reasons": "Tabrisi says he should not toil so intensely; Qurtubi associates this reading with the Prophet's swollen feet and Gabriel's advice that his body has rights, framing the mission as an easy upright religion. Ibn al-Munir objects that this makes hardship the reason for revelation and conflicts with the consolation of 18:6; Alusi says the intended sense removes that conflict. {"id": "20:7/q01", "question": "What does it mean to speak aloud?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:7/q01/p1", "position": "It means raising the voice so speech is audible, as opposed to hushed speech.", "reasons": "Jishumi contrasts voiced sound with whispering; Tabrisi supplies the verb and participial forms; Ibn al-Jawzi applies it to Moses' effort; al-Alusi applies it to speech and al-Tabataba'i contrasts jahr with israr."}]}
{"id": "20:7/q02", "question": "Whom does the conditional address?", "turns_on": "Whether the second person singles out the Prophet or is indefinite and general.", "positions": [{"id": "20:7/q02/p1", "position": "It addresses Muhammad, with the teaching extending to his community or all people.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari includes the Prophet's private and public speech; Ibn Atiyya extends Muhammad's address to human speech to others or idols; Abu Hayyan calls the Prophet the apparent addressee; al-Bahr, cited by Alusi, includes his community; Ibn Ashur includes others."}, {"id": "20:7/q02/p2", "position": "It addresses humanity without singling out a particular person.", "reasons": "Alusi allows a general human address, and Ibn Ashur says an indefinite second person reaches everyone."}]}
{"id": "20:7/q03", "question": "What speech does al-qawl include here?", "turns_on": "Whether the definite noun takes all speech or the contextual act of addressing God.", "positions": [{"id": "20:7/q03/p1", "position": "Speech broadly, including recitation, supplication, remembrance, and ordinary conversation.", "reasons": "Alusi reports a broad sense; Ibn Ashur defines qawl as a verbal noun for utterance and says recitation is particularly relevant after 20:2; Ibn Atiyya includes speech addressed to other people or idols."}, {"id": "20:7/q03/p2", "position": "Remembrance or invocation addressed to God, especially loud recitation.", "reasons": "Al-Mufaddal, Tabrisi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Ashur relate it to reciting without strain; Zamakhshari, Baydawi, Bursevi and Alusi treat voiced remembrance and supplication; Alusi reports the contextual definite article argument. {"id": "20:7/q04", "question": "How does the conditional clause work?", "turns_on": "Whether an unspoken alternative or answer is supplied, or the stated answer itself asserts universal knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "20:7/q04/p1", "position": "The jussive condition has 'He knows the secret and more hidden' as its answer, expressing an invariable fact, not knowledge caused by speech.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas identifies the jussive and answer; Alusi denies temporal contingency; Ibn Ashur adduces conditionals by Abu Kabir, Bashama ibn Hazn, Ibrahim ibn Kunayf, and al-Qutami to show universal force."}, {"id": "20:7/q04/p2", "position": "An omitted parallel clause yields 'whether you speak aloud or not, He knows the secret and more hidden.'", "reasons": "The Nazm author, Tabrisi, and Islahi make the omitted alternative explicit; Wahidi notes why the stated contrast initially seems unusual."}, {"id": "20:7/q04/p3", "position": "An omitted answer means 'do not strain yourself'; the stated knowledge supplies its reason.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur supplies the apodosis from the knowledge assertion and the Prophet's effort to recite aloud."}, {"id": "20:7/q04/p4", "position": "The condition implies 'know that God knows your loud speech as well as the hidden.'", "reasons": "Alusi gives this expansion; Ibn Ashur says loudness adds nothing to God's prior knowledge."}]}
{"id": "20:7/q05", "question": "Why mention loud speech when God knows the secret?", "turns_on": "Whether the conditional chiefly argues from the hidden, guides the Prophet's vocal effort, cautions speakers, or recalls a dispute about God's hearing.", "positions": [{"id": "20:7/q05/p1", "position": "Knowing what is most hidden proves all the more that God knows audible speech; volume adds nothing to His hearing.", "reasons": "Mawardi frames 'why speak aloud?' as a question; the Nazm author, Wahidi, Razi, Abu Hayyan, Tabataba'i, and Study Quran use inference from hidden to audible; Bagawi and Tabrisi stress the greater hidden degree; Ibn Ashur notes secret speech is especially hard for humans to know."}, {"id": "20:7/q05/p2", "position": "It reassures or counsels the Prophet not to strain in loud recitation or supplication, since God hears without it.", "reasons": "Al-Mufaddal, Tabrisi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Biqai and Ibn Ashur apply it to recitation; Islahi says God hears the Prophet's pleas in every state and will guide him for his benefit, with 19:64."}, {"id": "20:7/q05/p3", "position": "It can warn speakers against evil public speech, since God hears it.", "reasons": "Alusi says public speech is singled out because most conversation is aloud."}, {"id": "20:7/q05/p4", "position": "It alludes to a dispute over whether God hears quiet speech and answers the doubters.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur relates the Ibn Masud report near the Kaaba, links 41:22 and 11:5, and says this context explains the seemingly unusual choice of loud speech."}]}
{"id": "20:7/q06", "question": "What guidance does the verse give about audible remembrance or supplication?", "turns_on": "How 7:205 and the restraint reports relate to sound reports of aloud remembrance, and whether loudness is moderate, excessive, or serves a purpose.", "positions": [{"id": "20:7/q06/p1", "position": "Aloud remembrance is allowed or recommended when useful and free of harm; excessive volume is discouraged.", "reasons": "Baydawi and Alusi give imprint, focus, humility and protection from distraction; Biqai allows volume to make others hear. Alusi cites over twenty sound reports, the Prophet's voiced prayer formula for teaching, Shafi'i preference with apparent Hanbali and Maliki support, the two Hanafi companions' Eid takbir, and al-Kurani's defense. He treats funeral dislike as contextual, the Ibn Masud group-dhikr report as unsound or about excess, and Abu Hanifa's reports as different degrees of volume. {"id": "20:7/q08", "question": "What are 'the secret' and 'what is more hidden'?", "turns_on": "Whether concealment is measured against other people, one's present awareness, future unknown acts or thoughts, forgotten thoughts, or God's own undisclosed knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "20:7/q08/p1", "position": "The secret is a present inward thought or concealment; the more hidden is future thought, action, or event unknown to the person now.", "reasons": "Sa'id, Qatada and Ibn Abbas distinguish what one knows now from what has not entered the mind or occurred; Ibn Abbas says one divine knowledge encompasses past and future and cites 31:28. Ibn Kathir reports al-Dahhak and Mujahid too; Wahidi says this is the majority view. Tustari specifies a thought arriving in sleep. Sulami's Fudayl says what one will know tomorrow; al-Wasiti says what God has not commanded to exist. Razi permits future divine acts; Tabari's Ibn Abbas report distinguishes completed deed from an unacted prompting; Durr cites al-Hakim's authentication of one Ibn Abbas report. Kuranyolu attributes to Tabari a preference for possible things God has not created or disclosed, whereas Qurtubi's attribution to Tabari favors future human thought."}, {"id": "20:7/q08/p2", "position": "The secret is something confided quietly to another; the more hidden is a thought or matter kept within oneself.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan, Ibn Abbas, Ikrima and al-Farra distinguish private speech from inner thought; Zamakhshari and Nasafi add a possible later inward concealment. Ibn Ashur locates the comparison in inner speech quieter than a whisper. Tabataba'i accepts the whispered report as speech but says a true secret is kept within oneself."}, {"id": "20:7/q08/p3", "position": "The secret is a deed concealed from people; the more hidden is inner whispering.", "reasons": "Mujahid's explanation recurs through Tabari, Thalabi, Mawardi, Bagawi, Tabrisi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Kathir and Durr; Thalabi also reports Ibn Abbas identifying the most hidden with self-talk."}, {"id": "20:7/q08/p4", "position": "God knows creatures' secrets and has hidden His own secret from them.", "reasons": "Zayd ibn Aslam and Ibn Zayd are repeatedly cited. Zamakhshari rejects this, Ibn Atiyya calls its past-verb construction weak, Qurtubi reports Tabari's rejection, and Alusi and Tabataba'i reject or disfavor it. Razi compares 2:255 and Samīn compares 20:110; al-Tabrisi gives the past-verb construction. Kuranyolu's attribution to Tabari concerns uncreated possibilities and differs from Qurtubi's attribution."}, {"id": "20:7/q08/p5", "position": "The secret is an inward intention or settled resolve; the more hidden is a subtler prompting not yet resolved or formed.", "reasons": "Mawardi and Bagawi distinguish resolve from impulse; Razi offers both formed resolve versus unformed notion and unconceived thought; Abu Hayyan reports a settled intention versus what has not entered the heart. Burhan places promptings beyond imagined whispers."}, {"id": "20:7/q08/p6", "position": "The secret is inwardly concealed thought; the more hidden is a thought that arose and was forgotten.", "reasons": "Al-Baqir and al-Sadiq are cited by Tabrisi, Alusi and Tabataba'i; Tabataba'i also gives Abu Abd Allah's report through Muhammad ibn Muslim."}, {"id": "20:7/q08/p7", "position": "The secret is an unspoken conscious thought; the more hidden reaches the subconscious or unconscious.", "reasons": "Asad gives conscious versus subconscious; Kuranyolu cites Esed on the same distinction."}, {"id": "20:7/q08/p8", "position": "The secret is anything the human mind can contain; the more hidden is divine knowledge beyond human access.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya reports a group including possible future thoughts within the human side; Zajjaj says the further unseen is known to God alone."}, {"id": "20:7/q08/p9", "position": "The secret is an inspiration latent in the heart's core; the more hidden remains concealed until its manifestation begins.", "reasons": "Sulami places the inspiration beyond senses, reason, angels and devils, unfolding through will and decree; an explanation reported by Alusi compares it to fire latent in damp wood, stirred by will."}, {"id": "20:7/q08/p10", "position": "The secret and the more hidden are God's nested secrets within a person.", "reasons": "Sulami reports Junayd's formulation."}, {"id": "20:7/q08/p11", "position": "The secret is what a person does not disclose; the more hidden is what only that person has said to themself.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba defines undisclosed sirr and self-confided akhfa; Majaz makes akhfa self-confiding kept from everyone and cites the poet's awhad for a non-comparative elative. Bursevi includes unspoken and future thoughts as other possibilities."}, {"id": "20:7/q08/p12", "position": "God knows audible speech, what people conceal within, and deeds they do without realizing He knows them.", "reasons": "Muqatil distinguishes the person's concealment from their unawareness of God's knowledge."}]}
{"id": "20:7/q09", "question": "How is akhfā construed grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the form is an elative with an omitted comparison, a non-comparative elative, or a past verb; transmitted explanations and poetic usage are weighed.", "positions": [{"id": "20:7/q09/p1", "position": "It is a comparative or superlative adjective, 'more hidden than the secret,' with the comparison understood.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas and Tabrisi supply 'than it'; Burhan and Itqan discuss omitted comparands and af'al outside predicate position; Razi, Abu Hayyan, Samin, Ibn Ashur, and Tabataba'i take the elative. Ibn Atiyya calls it weak; Zamakhshari, Alusi and Tabataba'i reject or disfavor it."}, {"id": "20:7/q09/p3", "position": "It is an elative used without comparison, meaning simply 'hidden.'", "reasons": "Majaz and Wahidi cite a poet's awhad meaning 'one'; Abu Ubayda cites al-Farazdaq's 'more noble and taller' for plain noble and tall. {"id": "20:7/q10", "question": "Why place 'more hidden' after 'the secret'?", "turns_on": "Whether the order is explained by semantic emphasis or the verse ending; Burhan records both.", "positions": [{"id": "20:7/q10/p1", "position": "The ascending degree of hiddenness emphatically displays God's penetrating knowledge.", "reasons": "Burhan calls the wording more emphatic; Tabataba'i says movement from audible to secret to most hidden proves knowledge of all, even an intention hidden from its thinker; Kuranyolu says the pair conveys penetration of every detail; Razi divides the three levels."}, {"id": "20:7/q10/p2", "position": "The order preserves the verse ending or rhyme.", "reasons": "Burhan offers the verse ending alongside the comparative analysis and notes reversal of an expected order; Itqan gives the same reason."}]}
{"id": "20:7/q11", "question": "What does the verse teach about God's knowledge?", "turns_on": "The notes develop the verse's omniscience as a doctrine of God's timeless attribute, moral accountability, or the source of human knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "20:7/q11/p1", "position": "God knows all open, hidden, past and future things without limitation, even what people cannot know of themselves.", "reasons": "Qashani and Asad include outward and inward states; Ibn Abbas reports compare all creation to one soul under one knowledge, citing 31:28. {"id": "20:7/q13", "question": "How does this verse connect to its surrounding passage and other verses?", "turns_on": "Whether the connection is the progression from dominion to knowledge, the source of revelation, or the larger Moses narrative.", "positions": [{"id": "20:7/q13/p1", "position": "After God's dominion and power, the verse establishes His comprehensive knowledge; together they establish sovereignty and lordship.", "reasons": "Razi and Alusi connect 20:5–6's power to 20:7's knowledge; Baydawi links complete attributes to their implications. {"id": "20:7/q16", "question": "How is the Qur'an's inimitability known?", "turns_on": "Whose knowledge is at issue, and whether recognition is immediate or follows inference from rhetorical incapacity.", "positions": [{"id": "20:7/q16/p1", "position": "Its miraculous status is established by inference, although its appearance through the Prophet is known necessarily.", "reasons": "Baqillani and Itqan report al-Ash'ari's distinction; Baqillani contrasts a directly seen miracle such as the sea parting with the premises and comparison of styles needed here."}, {"id": "20:7/q16/p2", "position": "A rhetoric expert knows necessarily his own inability to match it, then infers the inability of others; nonexperts know only by inference.", "reasons": "Baqillani explains that Qur'anic style has no counterpart in customary speech and differs from ordinary poetic skill. {"id": "20:14/q03", "question": "What does the name Allah convey here, and how does it relate to Hebrew naming?", "turns_on": "The name's theological force and the proposed cross-language relation.", "positions": [{"id": "20:14/q03/p1", "position": "Allah names the necessary existent, worthy of all praise and alone perfect in the divine names.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr makes knowledge of God's proper name Moses' first revealed matter and the basis of later rulings. {"id": "20:14/q11", "question": "What does 'for My remembrance' mean as the purpose or time of prayer?", "turns_on": "Whose remembrance the genitive denotes; whether lām marks purpose or time; whether dhikr means God, an owed prayer, scriptural mention, appointed time, or exclusive devotion.", "positions": [{"id": "20:14/q11/p1", "position": "Pray in order to remember God within prayer.", "reasons": "Mujāhid says the praying servant remembers the Lord; al-Ḥasan, al-Zajjāj and Ibn Qutayba say prayer necessarily contains remembrance, glorification or magnification. Asad calls conscious oneness prayer's deepest purpose. Iṣlāḥī stresses preservation of remembrance; Study Quran says frequent remembrance in prayer. Al-Ālūsī says the hadith does not compel this literal interpretation; some verifiers see make-up as an implication of prayer's general purpose."}, {"id": "20:14/q11/p3", "position": "Pray so that God remembers the worshipper with praise or reward.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī and al-Ālūsī report this. {"id": "20:14/q14", "question": "What is the rule for prayer missed through sleep or forgetfulness?", "turns_on": "The scope of the Prophetic command and whether number of missed prayers limits liability.", "positions": [{"id": "20:14/q14/p1", "position": "Pray the missed prayer upon remembering or waking, as its required makeup and sole expiation.", "reasons": "Reports through Anas, Abū Hurayra and others quote the Prophet and cite this verse; some include sleep and say no other expiation. Al-Zajjāj and Ibrāhīm allow sunrise or sunset. Ibn ʿAbbās applies the verse to a missed night prayer; al-Durr also reports Abū Juḥayfa, Ibn Masʿūd, ʿUbāda and the post-Khaybar episode. Al-Qurṭubī says forgetting cancels sin, not duty, whether one prayer or many; Abū Hurayra's report says its time is remembrance. Ibn Kathīr prefers the phrase's missed-prayer interpretation on these reports."}, {"id": "20:14/q14/p2", "position": "More than five forgotten prayers need not be made up.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī calls this an anomalous view contrary to the Prophetic report requiring makeup for one or many."}]}
{"id": "20:14/q15", "question": "What does the report's 'no other expiation' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase excludes substitutes for prayer or additional penalties for inadvertence.", "positions": [{"id": "20:14/q15/p1", "position": "Nothing clears the missed prayer except making it up.", "reasons": "Al-Khaṭṭābī's first reading of the report."}, {"id": "20:14/q15/p2", "position": "Forgetting adds no separate penalty beyond the prayer itself.", "reasons": "Al-Khaṭṭābī contrasts intentional missed Ramadan fasting and omitted pilgrimage rites, where compensation can be due."}]}
{"id": "20:14/q16", "question": "Does a deliberately abandoned prayer have to be made up?", "turns_on": "Whether a sinful missed obligation remains payable; how severe 'never makes it up' language is construed.", "positions": [{"id": "20:14/q16/p1", "position": "Yes; deliberate omission adds sin, but does not discharge the duty.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī gives the majority view, argues a fortiori from sleeper and forgetful person, says the general imperative covers later performance, compares an unpaid human debt and an intentionally missed Ramadan day, and explains that God's 'forgetting' means abandoning, not literal loss of knowledge (9:67, 59:19, 2:106). He reads Mālik's contrary wording as impossibility of restoring the past or severe warning; the weak Abū al-Muṭawwis fasting report is likewise warning, while sound reports require makeup and repentance. {"id": "20:14/q17", "question": "Does makeup follow the original time-bound prayer command or a new command?", "turns_on": "Whether an expired appointed time ends the original command's scope.", "positions": [{"id": "20:14/q17/p1", "position": "It rests on the renewed Prophetic command to pray upon remembering.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī says performance outside the appointed day or night does not fulfill the original command, citing 17:78; absent the Prophet's instruction, such prayer would gain no reward."}, {"id": "20:14/q17/p2", "position": "The general command to establish prayer still entails makeup after its time.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī also invokes the imperative's general obligation without distinguishing on-time and late performance."}]}
